## 2026-09-14 — Lane E: a queued web write survives navigation (S29)

Implemented LLP 3000.007 §20.4 against base
`33b530d41b00f1d685656f360e37c52ec1255ad6`. Read the inventory's S29,
the 0.2.12 run's epoch 1789409378 and `m3-choreo.txt` (under its
0.2.11-named lane directory), and the 0.2.6 Astra diary's M3: both
builders routed administrative writes around the local client to survive
navigation. The Node reproduction uses fake page events, the real wasm
device, and a real `snapback4 dev` HTTP server. Before the fix it measured
2 durable admissions, 0 exit requests, 0 server rows before reopen, and
2 rows only after reopening the device. After the fix it measured 2 exit
requests and 2 rows before reopen; explicit duplicate HTTP requests and
reopening with the same mutation IDs left exactly 2 rows.

The web device already awaited `save` before returning an admission, and
IndexedDB `save` already awaited transaction completion. Its read/write
transactions now request strict durability. A synchronous view of committed
outbox entries changes only after a successful save; a failed save stops
further device calls so a drained but uncommitted admission cannot leak
into either transport. Pagehide and hidden visibility dispatch committed
unsent writes with authenticated fetch keepalive, without the ordinary
client's abort signal. Closing unregisters the hooks without cancelling
requests already dispatched. No Node process-device or Expo implementation
changed. The synchronous web hook advances the device send revision before
each dispatch wave, so a sync already in flight cannot apply an older
receipt on a resumed page; metadata persistence stays ordered behind any
current IndexedDB transaction. Settlement stays with ordinary sends and
sync receipts, so the next page reuses the same mutation IDs.

Keepalive counts UTF-8 JSON body bytes across these clients in the same
module instance. The test measured 64,082 bytes across 2 concurrent
requests against the 65,536-byte browser budget; 2 further requests
(including another client's) dispatched as quota was released. Larger
queues split into waves while the page can still run. A single atomic
mutation over 65,536 bytes cannot be split across the existing `/m`
endpoint, and the page may disappear before a subsequent wave starts;
those entries remain durable for ordinary sends or reopening. Other page
libraries can also consume the browser quota. Beacon is not a fallback:
it cannot attach the endpoint's bearer/persona headers and shares the
keepalive quota. The README and writes card state the bounded behavior.
No E_/N_ code or diagnostic text was added or changed.

performs a full navigation to about:blank, queries the server before

## 2026-10-12 — ROLL: retaining rollback and hot release activation

Release adoption now separates active shapes from dormant tables/cells/index definitions. Older writes preserve retained cells; new rows get candidate literal defaults/nulls on restoration, while enum, required-value, ownership and lifetime conflicts name affected rows and refuse atomically. Removal requires explicit `prune --allow-destructive`, with durable audit/history. `rollback --to N` deliberately restores immutable source. Release stores get a format fence; device/development stores retain their existing format.

An admitted `serve` owns hot deploy over a private same-owner socket. Source/native/worker preparation precedes the transaction; reader/runtime/generation publication shares the writer guard. Native wasm content changes advance semantic generation even when declarations are unchanged. Worker preparation is revision-bound, including named additions/removals. Lost replies and stale convenience pointers recover from the database. LLP 3000.000.000 and SERVER.md own the design and operations; the OPS deploy card points there. ## 2026-10-12 — Lane EX: the meter charges only live rows; a refusal after an unproved insert defers to the server

Two findings of the widened generator (LLP 3000.035 §5.1), branch
`sb4/device-meter-expiry`.

- **Ruling A (Charlie, 2026-10-08), LLP 3000.007 §20.24.6.** The public meter
  charges only rows live at the read's clock. The server's scans charged an
  expired row the sweep had not removed (examined, then steps and heap), which
  the device never received, so meters diverged and low ceilings cut on the
  server where the device completed. Now `scan_authorized` (both paths, a
  system read through a new `live_store_scan`), the private authorization walk,
  the device's live recount and the server's maintained backlog read step over
  expired rows before any public charge. `Runner::step_expired` prices them on
  their own guard (256 B plus key per row, `E_STORE_MEMORY` past 256 MiB per
  execution) and returns their unit of the 8,192-row walk. One engine change
  covers SQLite, PostgreSQL, `MemoryRows` and both device stores.
- **Defect B, LLP 3000.007 §20.5.** A device predicted an insert over a hidden
  id or unique value, carried on, and refused locally later in the block
  (`E_CONSTRAINT`, `NOT_FOUND`, `E_OVERFLOW`), a final code the server never
  reports (it refuses `E_RULE` at the insert). Each authored plain device insert
  now runs the upsert insert-arm proof on the device allowance; after an
  unproved one, `predict` turns a later refusal into `E_PREDICT`, so the write
  queues and the server's refusal is reported. Provable refusals stay final.
- **Tests.** Four focused tests in `snapback4-difftest/tests/devices.rs` (server
  against both device stores at every boundary of every dimension; a cut before
  and after the sweep; the three refusal shapes queue; provable refusals stay
  local); all fail on the old engine. About thirty tests pinned the old model
  (expired rows charged, backlogs cutting reads or refusing `E_BOUND`, literal-id
  inserts refusing locally) and now state the new contract; where a backlog was
  only a device to force a cut, a rejected live row or a lower ceiling does it.
- **Harness (main's widened generator).** `run-devices --seed 0 --cases 20000`:
  0 read and 0 cut disagreements in 152,256 positions per store (the 14 expired-meter
  signatures per store are gone); writes: 11 named unique-key outcomes per store
  and 1 disagreement per store, the known insert beside an `upsert` branch
  (outside the named condition, recorded in the GW follow-up); the three
  `write-refused` signatures are gone. `run-stores --seed 0 --cases 5000` with a
  private PostgreSQL 17 cluster: 0 disagreements (128,202 positions per prefetch
  mode, 1,124 prelude, 3,964,936 SQLite repeats). The 30 retained device cases
  replay as resolved regressions (`pass`, or `prediction-declined` for the
  refusals).
- **wasm.** 646,316 → 646,816 B gzip (+500; budget 646,816 unchanged, zero
  headroom). The first spelling cost +2,363; compaction: a web device never reads
  as the system, so `live_store_scan` is SQLite-only; the step price is a fixed
  reservation, not a serialized row size; `device_work` split into non-generic
  enter/leave halves (−157 across its instantiations); B reuses
  `prove_upsert_insert` instead of a refactored proof; short messages.
- **What was surprising:** the meter used to carry a time-hidden existence bit
  (a word held only by an expired row cost a seek; a maintained backlog cost
  observable examined work). The ruling closes it; the attack witness in
  `expiring_mutations.rs` now shows the worlds agree even without the admission
  guard.
- **What was hard:** the collateral. Literal-id inserts into partitioned tables
  are common in tests, so B changed the expected outcome of every such test
  whose program refuses after the insert. The wasm budget had 500 B of room.

## 2026-10-16 — LANG2 P18: readability is part of a refusal proof

A private read rule can hide a target while its update rule admits the mutable
remainder; even a known immutable key mismatch is then ignored at runtime.
The hard-refusal fragment now requires unconditional public/allow readability
or a system job. Private policies get N_IMMUTABLE_PATCH unless an equal value
already makes the patch quiet. The source/native/simulator regression proves
that a hidden caller succeeds while the readable caller's mismatch refuses.
This source-diagnostic refinement preserves the existing runtime exception;
LLP 3000.036.002 §10 and its fresh reviews record the final boundary.

The readability proof also excludes opening/expiry, inherited read-through and
ephemeral lifetimes, including system jobs. A public rule alone does not make
an inactive target readable. The new pinned-clock regression covers an
unopened success and an opened immutable refusal; generated P18 coverage now
has 64 cases, including private-owner and unopened-public queues with explicit
post-settlement comparison classes.

Opaque expression blocks can assign caller locals even without table writes
(job `as` is one example). Immutable key/value, object, snapshot and minted-id
proofs now stop at those barriers. Native/simulator regressions execute both
the equal and differing literal cases and check that a stored id read inside
`as` never inherits the freshness of an overwritten local.

A proven fresh unused component of an upsert's unique identity establishes an
insert-only operation. Its initial immutable values stay quiet, including a
second minted id and creation clock. Ordinary insert constraints still apply;
a write or opaque effect after the capture prevents claiming this absence.

## 2026-10-20 — P1-ID step 2: Postgres identity access

The Postgres adapter implements `IdentityTransaction` on its existing `Tx` and
`IdentityStore` on a borrowed `RefCell<&mut Store>` family view. This keeps the
port's shared-reference contract while the driver keeps exclusive connection
custody for transaction creation. Signup/login credential checks, full/read
replacement, principal revocation and supervised-worker mint/clear/revoke use
the existing serialized shared-head transaction. Transaction-level identity
writes reuse authority's fence guard and refuse read-only/optimistic walks.
Read-only credential and diagnostic expiry queries use ordinary snapshots.

Attach adds principals, credentials, mint bindings (including scope) and worker
metadata with `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` after taking the existing head
lock. Text lookup keys use `COLLATE "C"`; integer facts use `BIGINT`. Existing
sessions, generations and read-session storage are reused. SQL preserves the
SQLite statement order, NULL family fallback, principal insert-ignore and
worker marker behavior. The versioned migration runner and P1b owner fence
remain separate work; no new fence or production-host capability is claimed.

Postgres smoke/fence tests are gated with the existing named isolated-database
skip; their real-cluster result follows below. The shared-family parity suite
is the next separately committed step.

(2 passed, 0 skipped); that owned cluster was stopped by its exit trap. The

## 2026-10-20 — P1-ID step 3: one identity contract on both adapters

Fourteen adapter-neutral identity cases now cover transaction facts and family
invalidation, credentials and read/full rotation rollback, each rotation
refusal, principal insert-ignore, exact credential lookup and byte ordering,
NULL family fallback, delete row counts, wide integer timestamps and captured
generations, mint binding persistence/collision rollback, worker isolation and
markers, and trusted/untrusted diagnostics. SQL and legacy-fixture setup stay
inside adapters. Diagnostics delegate to the same shared policy helper on both
stores; the public SQLite entry point and refusal text are unchanged.

Postgres adds four adapter witnesses: session/logout round trip, rejection of
every transaction-level write without the existing serialized head fence,
waiting for the head before invoking a mint callback, and installing missing
identity tables at attach/reopen while preserving session rows and explicit
C collations on lookup keys. The existing three shared authority tests run
alongside them. Every database test is explicitly ignored with a named reason
by the ordinary harness and requires `SNAPBACK4_EVAL_POSTGRES` when opted in;
missing environment or connection failure cannot count as a pass.

The new worker-marker case reproduced a real translation difference: SQLite
LIKE removes ASCII-case variants of `worker:family:` and `worker:status:`;
Postgres LIKE leaves them. Postgres now uses ILIKE on its C-collated metadata
key for these fixed ASCII prefixes. The case covers both variant family rows
and variant status keys. Other exercised differences are translated with
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, COALESCE, LEAST, u64 delete counts and BIGINT facts.
Postgres wraps convenience writes in head-fenced transactions; SQLite's
pre-existing non-atomic convenience insert/logout primitives retain autocommit.
Failure atomicity of those primitives is not a shared guarantee; rollback
assertions exercise the explicit atomic composites and caller-owned transactions.

## 2026-10-21 — K0b: member savepoints and explicit disposition

The reference committer owns the original fenced `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction.
Its body receives a borrowing `MemberTx` under `SAVEPOINT member`, retaining the
existing Tx surface through dereference. `commit(value)` releases only that
savepoint and selects Complete; `rollback(value)` selects Abort and rolls back
that frame. Normal early returns select Abort, and facade drop rolls back the
frame. Only the committer physically commits; Abort/error drops its owning Tx
and rolls back. Activation and Following keep the explicitly administrative
`run_solo` / `Solo::open_solo_with` path with their original shared transaction.

Mutation replay and input/asset refusals, empty job/timeline/view attempts, and
errors discard every provisional write, including the clock and metadata pins.
Program refusals retain their original receipt commit after `program` rollback;
job/timeline parking, private row-view chunks, clock-only/stale publication,
expiry, seed/deletion, load/restore, orphan repair, reset and the smoke barrier
retain their original commit points. All string literal multisets (including
SQL and error text) match the base in the nine changed producer/adapter files.
No host metadata caller, Postgres implementation or census allowance changes.

Job status reads, expiry continuation and its follow-on publication, and
timeline rotation run after the driver's physical COMMIT. Mutation's entropy
assignment also moves behind COMMIT; the current runner never mutates that
field, so its value is unchanged. Reset acknowledges only a Complete physical
commit. Activation's existing hooks and all downstream engine hooks still run
after COMMIT, including catalog/identity acceptance, narration, expiry state
clearing and ephemeral rebind. A sweep's fallible follow-on can still start its
own transaction and report failure after the sweep has durably committed.

Four SQLite witnesses beside the adapter cover two members in one physical
transaction, with member 1 completing and member 2 rolling back, dropping or
erroring; member 1 survives and member 2's writes and clock do not. Every nested
frame name is exercised, including lazy sequence-table rollback and member-local
change recording. Other cases distinguish normal Ok/Abort from Complete,
exercise a follow-on writer after COMMIT, and inject a deferred constraint
failure after successful savepoint release: no acknowledgement or hook runs.
The two solo hook tests remain. There is no production batching, continuation
protocol, queue or retry in this slice.

The required binary build and complete core run pass, including integrations
and all 17 doctests. The six final seam tests pass. The complete host run
executes every target with exactly the three expected inherited failures:
`w11r1c_toolchain_why_explains_node_start_failure_too` and
`farm2_typescript_7_is_refused_by_version_not_crashed_on` need TypeScript;
`web_witness_help_and_invalid_input` needs the built client JS. Both ratchets
pass with unchanged allowances (49 production openers; seven production and
95 test store-port sites). No allowance was raised or raise override used.

The required Clippy run retains the two errors reproduced at `94a91c9294` in
a second local detached worktree: `while_immutable_condition` in
`engine/read.rs` and `never_loop` in `engine/row_views.rs`. There are no new
warning sites/categories; redundant facade dereferences were removed. The
inherited native-helper argument-count lint falls from ten bindings to nine,
and its redundant Ok/question-mark lint disappears. No inherited lint was
suppressed or repaired. `ref-check` and `git diff --check` pass. Commands used

## 2026-10-20 — P1-JB task 2: one jobs contract on SQLite and Postgres

Moved the original shared cases to `engine/job/test_cases.rs` and expanded
that one suite; SQLite and Postgres supply transaction/savepoint lifecycle
and raw storage witnesses. Eleven shared lifecycle/inspection cases plus the
shared two-writer transition/assertions run on both adapters. SQLite has 12
family tests; Postgres has those 12 plus four attach/fence/generation witnesses,
for 16. Native coverage uses the default feature and checks exact JSON cursor
bytes, including whitespace, then empty bytes and NULL. Both race tests observe
the second writer actually waiting at the database lock before the first
commits; it reads the first committed cursor and advances it, leaving exactly
two chunks and two rows written, never a lost advancement.

SQLite/Postgres differences examined and resolved:

- FIFO heads use `(created_at, id)` in binary order. Newest-run lists instead
  retain SQLite's insertion tie order, made explicit with rowid; Postgres
  stores an insertion ordinal. Summary ties use descending id, and the
  64-row limit precedes name deduplication on both adapters.
- Postgres parameters require explicit BIGINT widths: sweep/chunk sizes above
  2^31, counters/retries/heap peaks above 2^53, i64 endpoint times and canonical
  integer JSON round-trip exactly. No float or JSONB conversion occurs.
- SQLite's cursor hex is an adapter encoding; Postgres BYTEA returns the same
  raw bytes and preserves NULL versus an empty cursor. Canonical args/domain
  text and the native cursor's original JSON bytes are compared physically.
- SQLite's error prefix counts characters while its truncation flag counts
  bytes. Postgres keeps that rule, including a multi-byte character crossing
  the byte cut, absent errors, zero limits and the signed cast of usize::MAX.
  The host retains the final UTF-8-safe byte cut. Negative cast job limits
  mean unlimited on SQLite; Postgres maps them to NULL LIMIT.
- SQLite LIKE folds the ASCII `schedule:` prefix, including a legacy uppercase
  metadata key. A live SQL probe confirmed Postgres LIKE did not; ILIKE restores
  parity. Exact per-schedule reads remain case-sensitive. Malformed and
  overflowing saved boundaries are skipped, and shape/other-family keys do
  not participate in the latest-boundary maximum.
- Missing-row park/finish/chunk writes succeed without creating rows on both
  stores. Park and finish preserve previously committed accounting; finish
  clears the cursor/upper while preserving the saved error, as SQLite does.

The first expanded private-cluster audit passed all 16 new Postgres tests and
all 12 SQLite family tests. Its Postgres module result was 50 passed / one
inherited failure: `reopening_legacy_maintained_ids_rebuilds_before_publishing_the_generation`
reinserts `groups/group` with `old=None` (23505). This is already tracked in
`issues/20261017-snapback4-postgres-legacy-maintained-id-fixture-inserts-existing-group.md`,
with unchanged-base reproduction; no unrelated fixture was edited. Running
all ignored tests also opted into the unrelated `cal18_projection` allocation
experiment, whose SQLite allocator setup was too late after other library
SQLite tests initialized it (SQLITE_MISUSE 21). Normal checks retain its named

## 2026-10-21 — P1-JB: embedded-NUL error parity and final validation

An additional live probe found that SQLite stores an error containing NUL,
keeps the entire string for job inspection, and stops substr's character
prefix at NUL while octet_length still counts every stored byte. Postgres
TEXT rejects NUL. The new Postgres jobs table therefore stores error strings
as UTF-8 BYTEA, decodes full errors losslessly, and fetches at most four bytes
per requested summary character before clipping an incomplete last character
and applying SQLite's NUL/character boundary. The SQL preflight also bounds
its byte count before multiplying, so very large requested limits cannot
overflow. The shared summary case now covers NUL, empty versus absent errors,
and prefixes whose byte window ends inside a four-byte character. This is
storage encoding only; job errors still have the same String/Option surface.

The complete normal core check passed before this last error-only adapter
change; final affected family cases are rerun for both adapters below. The
registration lines in postgres/mod.rs were moved away from P1-RQ's insertion
points; store.rs remains unchanged, and the authority helper visibility change
is identical to P1-RQ's. No second worker or other checkout was used.

Final validation (2026-10-21): `cargo test -p snapback4-core` and the normal
`cargo test -p snapback4-core --features postgres` both pass, including every
integration target and doc tests; the latter ran with the owned private
cluster configured. After the late error-encoding fix, the final affected run
`cargo test -p snapback4-core --features postgres --lib jobs -- --include-ignored`
passes 28/28: 12 SQLite and 16 Postgres, native included, zero skips. This final
run includes embedded/leading NUL, empty errors and byte windows cutting a
four-byte character. Without SNAPBACK4_EVAL_POSTGRES, the final Postgres family

`cargo test -p snapback4 --test store_port_ratchet` passes 5/5. The exact

## 2026-10-21 — P1-JB fix round 1: adapter parity after blind review

Rebased both lane commits onto main-mirror 1791e1a22b. Conflicts in the RFC,

Attach now refuses incompatible existing jobs storage with SNAPBACK_JOBS_SCHEMA,
including error TEXT with NULL or non-NULL data. Required shape/default/key
facts are checked under the attach head lock; compatible extra columns remain
allowed. Explicit cached projections survive a second connection's additive
upgrade. No per-operation writer contains DDL.

JobTransaction's shared policy rejects NUL in new ids/names and new schedule
names. Schedule existence is a raw key fact (even malformed saved boundaries
count), preserving updates to legacy SQLite rows; existing job updates never
revalidate their keys. Postgres NUL-key lookups short-circuit without a driver
query. Both park paths normalize U+0000 to U+FFFD before storage and summary
truncation, replacing this lane's superseded NUL-preservation behavior.

Shared chunk accounting reads totals under the current writer and saturates
at i64::MAX before writing absolute integers. This applies to Quarry/native
chunks, unsigned increments, retries and heap peaks; SQLite cannot promote an
addition to REAL and Postgres cannot overflow BIGINT. Oversized unsigned
row limits explicitly clamp to i64::MAX; summary prefixes clamp to i32::MAX
on both stores. A probe of the older host SQLite found a 32-bit substr length
wraparound; the repository's bundled SQLite uses 64 bits, but the explicit
32-bit prefix bound is portable across both and Postgres. Zero remains zero. The explicit SQLite rowid / Postgres
insertion ordinal tie ordering is retained and noted as an allowed SQLite ordering change in the RFC.

The shared real-statement-error case duplicates a job primary key after a
successful job and schedule write. The owner propagates the adapter error and
drops the transaction before commit; earlier writes vanish and later work
requires a fresh transaction. SQLite's driver can continue after some statement
errors, but callers may not do so under §9.1 rule 4. The separate successful
savepoint/refusal case remains useful and is not presented as error evidence.

Validation follows below. All cargo commands use four build jobs, incremental
disabled and dev/test line-table debug info, with one lane-owned cargo command
at a time. No other lane, git config, stash or push is used.

## 2026-10-21 — Lane NUL: identity and Postgres bind chokepoints

Commissioned on `40f97480c7` over `805fb4599a`. The identity/requests reviews
found more admission doors after three identity rounds and two request
rounds. The owner asked for a shape/bind boundary instead of another list of
entry-point patches (LLP 3000.009.001.000 §9.1).

`identity_fits` now rejects U+0000; `is_service` includes that shape check,
and `valid_name` already excludes it. Request/invocation ids, route viewers,
action workers and scheduled seats inherit the refusal from their existing
checks. Direct effect claims now check the worker shape before opening a
writer, ahead of expiry. Their SQLite engine tests assert no `total_changes`
even with a running expired lease plus queued work, so a refusal cannot
silently requeue work or invalidate its delegated session. Existing refusal
codes stand. Jobs and outbox adapters are untouched.

The Postgres `Tx::query`/`execute` path inspects typed parameter encodings
before Bind/Execute, including optional text and text arrays. It returns
`RuntimeError::Input` / `E_INPUT` for NUL while preserving a usable
transaction. `execute` validates before flushing buffered bookkeeping. A
physical test retains a pending commit across refusals and then commits it;
bytea zero bytes, optional NULL, arrays with NULL elements and JSON-escaped
NUL still work. Cold statement preparation may run before parameter checking;
no refused Bind/Execute is sent. Optional identity, request, receipt and row
lookups use the single `absent_text_key` helper and return absent without a
database call; missing principal generations retain their zero default.
Impossible request-name filters select no rows, and mixed name sets keep
the valid names.

Lost-delivery recovery once again asks for a live family member, then checks
that the family and member contain no NUL. It no longer substitutes the
full/action-authority walk for the parent's membership test. The same
transaction policy now has adapter tests for an `action`-kind bound session
and a family whose full session has closed while a read member remains.
Both replacements retain the original expiry and invalidate the previous
family members. The public SQLite entry retains validation before opening
its writer and samples its clock only after acquiring it.

Coverage boundary: `PostgresEngine` still explicitly refuses actions, routes,
effect workers and schedules as engine surfaces. The SQLite tests exercise

identity predicates without database calls, the landed identity/request
transaction capabilities, and the physical bind fallback. This does not
claim end-to-end Postgres engine coverage for unlanded families. The two
bound-session recovery cases run the same shared transaction policy on both
stores. Stored NUL identity authentication remains covered by the existing
SQLite legacy fixtures; PostgreSQL cannot store those rows.

The RFC's single Revised line prepends “NUL chokepoints”. Rule 1 now states
the shared shape checks, fail-closed stored identities, admission-only
validation in other families, absent Postgres lookups, the typed bind guard,
U+FFFD diagnostics and safe JSON. It explicitly retains ordinary expiry's
cleanup of an expired stored NUL session (Sol P3), and records the residual:
a direct Rust-API non-identity NUL write may store on SQLite and receive

## 2026-10-21 — K0c, frame boundary

The member facade now exposes only rows and narrow store-family methods.
Owning transaction dereference, raw connection access and physical abandon are
gone; nested frame names have a four-name allowlist. Disposition tokens are
opaque and the driver checks their agreement with the frame before COMMIT.
Reset's SQL stays in the adapter behind fixed reset operations. Two new tests
check the actual facade's absent escapes and forged contradictory dispositions.
The binary builds; continuation conversion and full verification follow in the
next K0c commit. SAVEPOINT + RELEASE remains two SQLite statements per completed
member, an accepted inherent cost, with a lone-member optimization deferred.


## 2026-10-21 — K0c, owned continuations

Every K0a/K0b hook now runs as a committer continuation with owned pending data.
Job ids become status reads after COMMIT; expiry installs its cursor then submits
a new publication member; timeline rotates and mutation installs entropy only
for completed members. Solo activation carries its report/catalog/identity into
acceptance, followed by narration and engine state acceptance. Reset carries its
owned result into expiry/scheduler/ephemeral changes and the caller reply. The
host's central durable wake body now runs through the same continuation runner,
with its existing selection, guard, state update and notification order. This
changes only that producer body in the host metadata lane's file.

Continuation failures use a distinct `RuntimeError::Continuation` wrapper, with
the original text, refusal envelope, retryability and busy classification. A
body or COMMIT error never runs one. The committer borrows its host separately
for execution and continuation, so a follow-on writer enters through a fresh
member. Solo adapter/engine acknowledgement stages also enter the runner; no
`after_commit` hook API remains. No production batching, queue or retry is added.

## 2026-10-21 — P1-AS: one asset ledger contract on SQLite and Postgres

The shared asset cases now run on both adapters: immutable declarations,
conditional publication/no-op conflicts, owner-scoped quota and recovery,
exact 128 MiB admission boundaries, BIGINT values beyond 2^53 and at i64::MAX,
aggregate overflow with rollback, placement/refusal/replay, view insert-ignore,

256-row batches and a zero-duration budget. Both stores exercise byte ordering,
51-row recovery lookahead and cached reads after additive columns. The SQLite
fixtures retain legacy NUL-key publication, replay, settlement, cancellation,
view and collection access. New NUL keys fail admission in shared policy;
Postgres NUL-key lookups are absent without a driver call. A NUL recovery
cursor is an ordering bound: its prefix gives the same comparison against
Postgres's NUL-free keys. No raw diagnostic text is stored in this family;
JSON facts, placements and terminal receipts already escape NUL.

Every applicable port RFC section 9.1 rule has a witness. Bounded selections
have total orders; prepared statements have explicit columns; statement
errors end the transaction by contract and the tests immediately drop/roll
back; counts/limits stay typed (the inventory limits are fixed positive
constants); installation and incompatible-shape refusals happen at attach.
Postgres writer tests hold their transaction while a peer obtains compatible
relation locks on all four tables, and every writer refuses a transaction
without the serialized head fence. Cancellation-first and publication-first
races use store/test_race.rs on both adapters. The holder keeps its fence
until the contender's SQLite busy handler fires or pg_blocking_pids reports
the holder. No race is inferred from a barrier or a harness SQL update.

Dialect differences are explicit: PostgreSQL SUM(bigint) is NUMERIC, so the
adapter casts the exact sum to BIGINT; both aggregate overflow paths roll
back. The shared quota comparison uses checked addition. The required
cancellation-state read preserves SQLite's QueryReturnedNoRows variant;
nullable declarations and tombstones stay distinguishable from absent rows.
Unknown kinds, partial home triples and legacy signed integer casts preserve
SQLite's reader behavior. SQLite's rowid TEXT primary key can hold a raw NULL
asset id, while the typed port requires String on both stores; PostgreSQL
therefore makes that key NOT NULL. Extra uniqueness, constraints, defaults,
triggers or row security refuse SNAPBACK_ASSET_SCHEMA instead of silently
changing typed operation outcomes. Fingerprints and JSON text stay unchanged.

## 2026-10-21 — P1-MR: bounded Postgres change evidence
